curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: Deliberate `.`, `;`/`,` plus `.`, `n`/`N` plus `.`, `@:`, `&`, `:~`; count vs repeat; repeat-friendly cursor placement
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Design one change that can be replayed across nearby or searched instances, and recognize when repeat is the wrong tool
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Change one field and repeat on later rows; search for a token and apply the same edit; compare `3dd` with repeated `dd`; rerun a recent Ex change
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core. `@:`, `&`, and `:~` bridge into Arc 3 and appear only after basic Command-line use

lessons.title: One change, many uses
lessons.objective: Treat dot as a deliberate replay of the last complete change.

activities.title: Dot repeats a change, not your journey
activities.body: The dot command replays the last complete text change from the cursor's new location. Motions used only to reach that location are not included.
activities.contrast: `j` chooses the next line; `.` repeats the edit there.

activities.title: Escape seals an inserted change
activities.body: An Insert-mode edit becomes repeatable when you return to Normal mode. Dot remembers the entry command, the literal text, and the exit as one change.
activities.contrast: Pressing dot while the first change is unfinished cannot replay it.

activities.title: Finish three declarations
activities.instruction: Append a semicolon once, then replay that complete change on the next two lines.

commandGroups.explanation: Append once and finish the change.

hints: Make the first append reusable.
Use `A` to append at the line end, then leave Insert mode.
After `A;Escape`, use `j.` twice.

feedback.why: Dot replayed `A;Escape`; the preceding `j` motions remained separate.

provenance.languageRationale: TypeScript declarations make missing terminators realistic while differing lengths prove that A is repeat-friendly.

activities.title: Promote every cache mode
activities.instruction: Change the first `draft` to `ready`, then replay on the next rows.
hints: Make one structural quote change.
Use `ci'`, enter `ready`, and escape.
Type `ci'ready Escape j . j .`.

feedback.why: The quote text object made a self-contained change that dot could replay.

activities.portability: Core Vim quote-object and dot behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Python configuration-like assignments give quote objects a natural use.

activities.title: Terminate the builder calls
activities.instruction: Add the missing semicolon to each call with one append and two repeats.

commandGroups.explanation: Apply it to both remaining calls.

hints: Use an entry command that finds the end for you.
`A` is replayed as part of the change.
Use `A;Escape j . j .`.

feedback.why: Because `A` belongs to the recorded change, differing line lengths do not matter.

provenance.languageRationale: Java method calls make semicolon insertion idiomatic and visibly useful.

activities.title: Enable every service
activities.instruction: Change all three aligned `false` values to `true`. Prepare the change once.
hints: Make the value edit one repeatable unit.
Change the word under the cursor and leave Insert mode.
Use `ciwtrue Escape j . j .`.

feedback.why: One word change supplied the recipe; line motions selected later instances.

provenance.languageRationale: Go short declarations provide compact repeated values without extra syntax.

lessons.title: Make the change repeatable
lessons.objective: Choose changes whose own motions and final cursor position survive variation.

activities.title: Put navigation inside the change when it belongs there
activities.body: A repeat is robust when the change can find its own boundary. Commands such as `A`, `I`, and text objects adapt to each new line or object.
activities.grammar: stable target → self-contained change → useful landing
activities.contrast: An absolute column may work once and fail when the next line is longer.

activities.title: Complete a Python mapping
activities.instruction: Append a comma to each mapping row, despite their different lengths.
hints: Let the change find each line end.
Append with `A`, not a fixed horizontal motion.
Use `A,Escape j . j .`.

feedback.success: The mapping rows now end cleanly.
feedback.why: Replaying `A,Escape` recalculated the end of every line.

provenance.languageRationale: Python mappings make trailing commas realistic and emphasize varied row lengths.

activities.title: Promote every environment
activities.instruction: Change each quoted `dev` value to `prod` by replaying one quote-object edit.
hints: Use the quotes, not columns, as the target.
Prepare `ci'prod` and escape.
Then use `j.` twice.

feedback.why: The text object adapts even though the YAML keys have different widths.

provenance.languageRationale: YAML keys naturally vary in width while quoted scalar values remain structural targets.

activities.title: Repair custom-property separators
activities.instruction: Replace each mistaken `=` with `:`. Let each repeated change land on the marked separator.

commandGroups.explanation: Find and replace the first separator.
Find the next separator and replay.

hints: Position on each `=` before replaying the replacement.
Use `f=r:` once; on later rows use `0f=` before dot.
Type `f=r: j0f=. j0f=.`.

feedback.success: Every declaration uses the intended separator.
feedback.why: The positioning commands were explicit; dot replayed only the one-character replacement.

activities.portability: Core character-find, replace, and dot behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: CSS custom properties provide realistic repeated separators at varying columns.

activities.title: Await every request
activities.instruction: Append `.await` to each expression with one repeatable change.
hints: Make the end-of-line motion part of the change.
Append `.await` with `A`, then escape.
Use `A.await Escape j . j .`.

feedback.why: Dot repeated the adaptive append instead of a fragile column-based edit.

activities.portability: The text edit is portable; whether `.await` is semantically valid depends on the host code.

provenance.languageRationale: Rust futures make repeated `.await` suffixes a familiar local transformation.

lessons.title: Find, change, echo
lessons.objective: Use character-find history to position dot-repeat across nearby instances.

activities.title: Repeat the search and the change separately
activities.body: After `f`, `F`, `t`, or `T`, semicolon repeats that character-find in the same direction and comma reverses it. Dot then repeats the prepared edit.

activities.title: Update settings in both directions
activities.instruction: Change the middle `old`, reverse to the first setting, then continue forward to the last.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the middle assignment and prepare the change.
Reverse past the current marker to the first value and replay.
Continue forward to the last value and replay.

hints: The last `f=` can travel in either direction.
Use `2,` to reach the first assignment and `2;` to reach the last.
Use `2f=lciwnew Escape 2,l. 2;l.`.

feedback.why: Comma and semicolon traversed the remembered `=` target; dot supplied the value change.

provenance.languageRationale: A neutral settings row makes forward and reverse character-find behavior explicit without language syntax distractions.

activities.title: Finish the CSV statuses
activities.instruction: Change the first `todo` to `done`, then use the remembered find to reach the others.

commandGroups.explanation: Find and change the first status.
Repeat the find and change twice.

hints: Find the `t` once and reuse that find.
After the first change, alternate `;` and `.`.
Use `ftciwdone Escape ; . ; .`.

feedback.why: Replacing `todo` removed the old `t`, so each semicolon advanced to the next untouched value.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; CSV is treated as neutral text.

provenance.languageRationale: CSV naturally exposes repeated fields on one line, ideal for semicolon traversal.

activities.title: Repair expression arrows
activities.instruction: Replace each mistaken `?` with `>` by finding the marker and replaying the replacement.

commandGroups.explanation: Find and repair the first marker.
Reuse the find on the next line, then dot.

hints: The previous `f?` can be repeated after returning to line start.
Use `j0;.` for each later line.
Type `f?r> j0;. j0;.`.

feedback.why: Semicolon reused the character target even across lines; dot reused the replacement.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the fragment is intentionally lexical rather than compilable C#.

provenance.languageRationale: C#-like member expressions provide varied prefixes around a repeated punctuation defect.

activities.title: Enable every shell flag
activities.instruction: Turn each `off` field into `on`, using `;` to revisit the remembered `=` target.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the first assignment and prepare the value change.
Reach and change the second value.
Reach and change the final value.

hints: Remember the `=` rather than searching for `off` repeatedly.
After the first value change, use `;l.`.
Use `f=lciwon Escape ;l. ;l.`.

feedback.why: The find target stayed stable while dot changed each following word.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the line is safe illustrative text and is not executed.

provenance.languageRationale: Shell-style assignments create a realistic compact row of repeated flag values.

lessons.title: Search, change, echo
lessons.objective: Use search history to carry one change through distant or bidirectional matches.

activities.title: Search chooses instances; dot changes them
activities.body: After `/` or `?`, `n` continues in the search direction and `N` goes the opposite way. Keep navigation and transformation separate: find a match, then press dot.
activities.contrast: `n` means same search direction, not always downward.

activities.title: Promote matching stages
activities.instruction: Search for `draft`, change one result, then continue through later matches.
hints: Search once; do not type the pattern again.
Change inside the first matched quotes, then use `n.`.
Use `/draft Enter ci"live Escape n . n .`.

feedback.why: Search history selected the distant values while dot replayed the quote change.

activities.portability: Core text search and dot behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: JSON gives repeated quoted values and a structurally clear target.

activities.title: Clean logs upward
activities.instruction: Search backward for `debug`, change it to `info`, then keep moving in that backward direction.
hints: With `?`, `n` continues upward.
Make one `ciwinfo` change, then repeat with `n.`.
Use `?debug Enter ciwinfo Escape n . n .`.

feedback.success: The log levels are cleaned upward.
feedback.why: `n` followed the original backward search direction.

provenance.languageRationale: Python logger calls are recognizable repeated search targets.

activities.title: Update rows on both sides
activities.instruction: Start at the middle `pending`, change it, continue forward, then use `N` to reach the remaining earlier match.

commandGroups.explanation: Reverse to the untouched earlier match.

hints: `N` reverses the search direction.
After changing the middle match, use `n.` and then `N.`.
Use `/pending Enter ci'active Escape n . N .`.

feedback.why: `n` and `N` selected matches in opposite directions; dot applied one transformation.

provenance.languageRationale: SQL predicate fragments make repeated status values realistic and direction-neutral.

activities.title: Normalize matching log codes
activities.instruction: Search for `E_TIMEOUT` and change every occurrence to `TIMEOUT` without touching `E_AUTH`.

commandGroups.explanation: Search only for the intended code.

hints: Use the precise code as the search anchor.
Change one matched word, then use `n.`.
Search `/E_TIMEOUT`, make `ciwTIMEOUT`, then replay twice.

feedback.why: A precise search kept the unrelated authentication record out of the workflow.

provenance.languageRationale: Logs naturally contain repeated codes separated by unrelated distractors.

lessons.title: Count or repeat?
lessons.objective: Choose between one counted change and several independently replayed changes.

activities.title: Counts commit; repeats let you inspect
activities.body: A count is compact when the number and adjacency are already certain. Separate repeats create separate changes and let you inspect or move between applications.
activities.contrast: Both can remove three lines, but they create different editing and undo histories.

activities.title: Dot remembers—and can replace—a count
activities.body: Without a new count, dot reuses the count from the last change. A count before dot replaces that remembered count for the replay.
activities.contrast: The count belongs to the change recipe, not to the movement between instances.

activities.title: Delete a known block
activities.instruction: Remove the three adjacent debug lines as one counted change.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete exactly three known adjacent lines.

hints: The rows are adjacent and the count is known.
Place the count before the line delete.
Use `3dd`.

feedback.why: A count was the lowest-setup tool for three certain adjacent lines.
feedback.contrast: `dd..` reaches the same text but creates inspectable separate changes.

provenance.languageRationale: Debug calls form a realistic fixed block whose size is obvious.

activities.title: Delete with inspection points
activities.instruction: Remove the three stale lines as three separate changes.

commandGroups.explanation: Replay twice, with a stop available after either dot.

hints: Make one line deletion, then replay it.
Use `dd`, followed by two dots.
Type `dd..`.

feedback.why: Repeated `dd` permits inspection or stopping between applications.

activities.portability: Core Vim dot and undo grouping behavior; this task validates text only.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral release notes keep attention on editing granularity.

activities.title: Reuse the deletion count
activities.instruction: Delete two temporary rows, then let dot reuse that count for the next pair.

commandGroups.explanation: Reuse the remembered count of two.

hints: Dot remembers the count attached to the change.
Make `2dd` the last change.
Then press `.` once.

feedback.why: Dot replayed the complete counted change `2dd`.

provenance.languageRationale: TOML-like flags make two temporary pairs and one keeper easy to distinguish.

activities.title: Replace the remembered count
activities.instruction: Delete two hashes first, then use a count before dot to delete the remaining three.

commandGroups.explanation: Replace the remembered count with three.

hints: A new count before dot replaces the old count.
After `2x`, replay deletion with a count of three.
Use `2x3.`.

feedback.why: `3.` replayed the deletion with three as its replacement count.

provenance.languageRationale: Markdown heading markers provide a visible run of identical characters for count replacement.

lessons.title: Replay the Ex line
lessons.objective: Use @: to execute the complete most recent Command-line command again.

activities.title: The colon register remembers the last Ex command
activities.body: `@:` executes the most recent Command-line command again. The replay includes the command text but runs at the current cursor and line context.
activities.contrast: Unlike dot, `@:` is specifically Command-line history and can replay Ex commands that dot does not represent clearly.

activities.title: Enable three feature flags
activities.instruction: Substitute `false` with `true` on the first line, then replay the Ex command on later lines.

commandGroups.explanation: Move and replay the Ex command.

hints: Replay the whole Command-line entry.
After the first substitution, move and use `@:`.
Use `:s/false/true/ Enter j @: j @:`.

feedback.why: `@:` reran the complete current-line substitution at each new row.

activities.portability: Requires Command-line history; hosts may reserve or incompletely emulate Ex behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: TypeScript feature flags make a repeated literal substitution obvious.

activities.title: Replace placeholder limits
activities.instruction: Change each `None` to `0` by replaying the first Ex command.

commandGroups.explanation: Replay it on both later lines.

hints: The entire substitution is in Command-line history.
Move down and execute the colon register.
Use `:s/None/0/ Enter j @: j @:`.

feedback.success: Every limit now has a numeric placeholder.
feedback.why: The same Ex command was valid in each line context.

provenance.languageRationale: Python commonly uses None as an unset placeholder, producing a natural literal edit.

activities.title: Activate selected rows
activities.instruction: Run one literal substitution per row by moving and replaying the last Ex command.
hints: Use one current-line substitution as the recipe.
Replay the Command-line with `@:` after each `j`.
Use `:s/draft/active/ Enter j @: j @:`.

feedback.why: `@:` is useful when the Ex command—not merely a Normal edit—is the reusable unit.

provenance.languageRationale: SQL value tuples provide repeated row-local literals without requiring range syntax.

activities.title: Lower every trace level
activities.instruction: Change each `TRACE` token to `INFO` by rerunning one Ex command.
hints: Reuse the latest Command-line entry.
The replay keys are `@:`.
Run `:s/TRACE/INFO/`, then `j@:` twice.

feedback.success: Every log level is now INFO.
feedback.why: The complete substitution was replayed without retyping it.

activities.portability: Requires Command-line history; the shell fragment is not executed.

provenance.languageRationale: Shell environment assignments are natural repeated line-local substitutions.

lessons.title: Repeat substitutions precisely
lessons.objective: Distinguish repeating the last substitution from combining it with the latest search.

activities.title: Ampersand repeats the substitution recipe
activities.body: In Normal mode, `&` repeats the last substitution on the current line. It reuses the search and replacement text, but previous substitution flags are not remembered.
activities.contrast: A prior `g` flag is dropped; use this fact deliberately rather than assuming it persists.

activities.title: Colon-tilde combines two histories
activities.body: `:~` uses the replacement from the last substitution with the most recently used search pattern. It matters only when a later search changed that pattern.
activities.contrast: `&` would still search for `cat`; `:~` uses `fox` and replaces it with `wolf`.

activities.title: Repeat a row-local rename
activities.instruction: Substitute `old` once, then use `&` on the later rows.

commandGroups.explanation: Apply it on the next two lines.

hints: Ampersand is a Normal-mode substitution repeat.
Move to a row and press `&`.
Use `:s/old/new/ Enter j & j &`.

feedback.why: `&` reused the last substitution pattern and replacement on the current line.

activities.portability: Core Vim substitution-repeat behavior; host emulators may vary.

provenance.languageRationale: Go-like field access gives a compact repeated literal rename.

activities.title: Observe the dropped global flag
activities.instruction: Replace both TODOs on the first line, then use `&` on the second line. Notice that only its first TODO changes.
hints: The first substitution needs `g`.
Plain `&` does not remember that flag.
Use `:s/TODO/DONE/g Enter j &`.

feedback.why: Ampersand reused the pattern and replacement but dropped `g`, so only the first second-line match changed.

activities.portability: This is native Vim behavior and requires explicit browser conformance.

provenance.languageRationale: Markdown task text makes multiple same-line TODO markers realistic and easy to inspect.

activities.title: Reuse a replacement with a new search
activities.instruction: Replace `cat` with `wolf`, search for `fox`, then apply the old replacement with `:~`.

commandGroups.explanation: Apply the old replacement to the latest search.

hints: Keep the replacement, change the search pattern.
After searching for `fox`, run `:~`.
Use `:s/cat/wolf/ Enter /fox Enter :~ Enter`.

feedback.success: Two patterns now share one replacement.
feedback.why: `:~` combined the latest search pattern `fox` with the last replacement `wolf`.

activities.portability: Native Vim behavior; some embedded hosts may not expose both histories correctly.

provenance.languageRationale: Plain prose makes the two independent search words unmistakable.

activities.title: Apply the live replacement to staging
activities.instruction: Change `draft` to `live`, search for `staging`, then use `:~` to reuse only the replacement.
hints: The new search and old replacement live in separate histories.
Search for `staging`, then run colon-tilde.
Use `:s/draft/live/ Enter /staging Enter :~ Enter`.

feedback.why: `:~` applied `live` to the most recently searched word.

activities.portability: Requires correct search and substitution history emulation.

provenance.languageRationale: YAML service stages provide two different values that naturally converge.

activities.title: Choose the exact substitution repeat
activities.instruction: Change `legacy` to `modern`, move down, and repeat that same substitution with `&`.

commandGroups.explanation: Apply it on the next line.

hints: The second line needs the same pattern and replacement.
Use ampersand, not colon-tilde.
Run the first substitution, then `j&`.

feedback.why: `&` was the precise tool because neither search nor replacement needed to change.

provenance.languageRationale: HTML class attributes are familiar repeated literals and make the unchanged recipe obvious.

lessons.title: Choose the smallest repeat tool
lessons.objective: Integrate repeat workflows and stop when the structure does not support safe replay.

activities.title: Repeat only what stays predictable
activities.body: Use a count for a known adjacent block, dot for one reusable Normal change, find or search to select repeated targets, and Ex history for a repeated Command-line recipe. Stop when instances need different judgment.
activities.contrast: A more advanced command is not safer when the structure is irregular.

activities.title: Search-driven annotation cleanup
activities.instruction: Search for `draft`, change the first annotation value, and repeat on later matches.
hints: Use search for selection and dot for transformation.
Prepare a quote-object edit on the first match.
Use `/draft Enter ci"live Escape n . n .`.

feedback.why: Search plus dot was lower setup than a macro and more inspectable than a broad substitution.

activities.portability: Core Vim search, quote-object, and dot behavior.

provenance.languageRationale: Kotlin annotations provide compact repeated quoted values and clear structure.

activities.title: Repair nearby separators
activities.instruction: Replace three `?` markers on one line by combining remembered find and dot.
hints: The punctuation is nearby and identical.
Find `?`, replace it, then alternate semicolon and dot.

feedback.why: Character-find plus dot was the smallest dependable local workflow.

activities.portability: Core Vim behavior; the initial fragment is intentionally malformed until corrected.

provenance.languageRationale: A C++ initializer makes nearby repeated separators visually obvious.

activities.title: Remove a fixed debug block
activities.instruction: Delete the three adjacent debug statements with the lowest-setup repeat tool.

commandGroups.explanation: Use one count for a known adjacent block.

hints: The rows are adjacent and already counted.
No search or replay setup is needed.
Use `3dd`.

feedback.why: A count was clearer than dot-repeat for a fixed adjacent block.

provenance.languageRationale: Swift debugPrint statements form a familiar fixed block.

activities.title: Replay the exact Ex recipe
activities.instruction: Change `draft` to `final` on three element lines by replaying the Command-line command.

commandGroups.explanation: Replay it on the remaining elements.

hints: The complete Ex recipe stays identical.
Use the colon register after each line motion.
Run the substitution once, then `j@:` twice.

feedback.why: `@:` directly expressed the repeated Command-line action.

provenance.languageRationale: XML element text supplies repeated line-local values without regex complexity.

activities.title: Know when to stop repeating
activities.prompt: Three similar handlers need different replacements based on business meaning: one retries, one reports, and one aborts. Which starting tool is safest?

options.label: Prepare one edit and press dot on every handler
Inspect and edit each handler deliberately

activities.explanation: The instances do not share one deterministic transformation. Blind repeat would encode a false assumption; semantic judgment belongs outside this repeat workflow.

activities.title: Design the replay before pressing dot
activities.body: Separate instance selection from transformation. Choose the smallest stable selector, make one self-contained change, and replay only while its assumptions remain true.
takeaways: Use counts for fixed adjacent work.
Use `;` or `,` for nearby character targets and `n` or `N` for search matches.
Use `@:` for the last Ex command, `&` for the last substitution recipe, and `:~` when the latest search supplies a new pattern.
Stop when repeated instances require different judgment.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last complete change at the cursor.
notes: Normal-mode motions used only for positioning are not repeated.
Without a new count, dot reuses the previous change count; a new count replaces it.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last character-find in the same or opposite direction.
notes: They move the cursor; combine them with dot to replay a change.

reference.purpose: Continue the latest search in the same or opposite direction.
notes: Same direction means the direction established by `/` or `?`, not always downward.

reference.purpose: Execute the most recent Command-line command again.
notes: The command runs in the current cursor and line context.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last substitution on the current line.
notes: The pattern and replacement are reused.
Previous substitution flags are not remembered.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last replacement using the latest search pattern.
notes: This combines substitution replacement history with search-pattern history.

reference.purpose: Choose a counted atomic change or inspectable repeated changes.
notes: Prefer a count for a known adjacent block.
Prefer repeat when movement or inspection separates applications.

coverage.concept: count vs repeat and dot counts
